material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Solvent S and extractant X are independent benchmark labels, not real substance identities. Equal indices across the two fields imply no shared identity or property. The catalog provides no material-property estimates.

dossier.identity_policy: Solvent and extractant IDs are independent benchmark-only labels and do not identify real materials. Equal codes across the two fields have no meaning.
dossier.interpretation_policy: Treat the marginal profiles as incomplete prior evidence. They cannot identify the best pair without controlled pairwise experiments and do not reveal the objective score or optimal process settings.

property_scope.extractant: Marginal nominal distribution and selectivity tendencies aggregated across an anonymous solvent reference panel.
property_scope.solvent: Marginal nominal distribution and selectivity tendencies aggregated across an anonymous extractant reference panel.

dossier.residual_policy: The solvent-extractant interaction table, world-level coefficient transform, phase-volume response, and mixing response are not disclosed. The hidden law is fixed for the entire campaign.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

# Partition study notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Target partition is governed by a solvent–extractant pairing-specific distribution tendency; the material dossier suggests, but does not establish, that S2 paired with X2 or X3 may give relatively high organic target fraction. A controlled pair screen at fixed phase amounts and mixing will test this. A result inconsistent with marginal rankings would support interaction-specific rather than additive behavior.

## H2 [tentative]
At fixed pairing and adequate equilibration, organic target fraction should increase with organic share of total two-phase volume, approximately as a distribution-ratio relation rather than as concentration alone. Pre-separation HPLC will be used because its organic/aqueous outputs are fractions of the fixed initial target inventory.

## H3 [tentative]
More vigorous or longer mixing should increase equilibration only until a plateau; a low-mixing condition may show incomplete transfer. A matched repeat is needed to distinguish numerical differences from noise.

## Retention prediction
After a two-phase reading, retaining the organic phase should preserve roughly the measured organic inventory and remove the aqueous inventory; retaining aqueous should do the converse. Final assay after explicit termination will test this, allowing for sampling/noise and without treating missing measurements as zero.

Planned scope: twelve independent batches from the same initial mixture, combining a controlled material-pair screen with phase-amount, mixing, repeatability, and opposite-retention tests. Anonymous IDs are categorical only.

# Partition study notebook

## H1 [supported in tested panel; interaction remains unresolved]
At fixed nominal recipe (0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous addition, 0.02 L extractant; 300 s at 600 rpm; 300 s settling), target partition depends materially on the categorical pairing. Pre-separation HPLC organic fractions ranged from about 0.493 to 0.615, larger than the stated 0.015 single-reading standard uncertainty. S2–X3 (event runner-operation-0037, 0.615) and S3–X2 (runner-operation-0067, 0.608) exceeded several other tested pairs, while S2–X2 was only 0.493 (runner-operation-0027). Thus equal or individually favorable marginal labels do not imply a favorable pair; a pairing interaction is plausible. The screen is sparse (7 of 16 pairs) and mostly unreplicated, so rankings within close differences remain uncertain.

## H2 [tentative; phase-volume test pending]
At fixed pairing and adequate equilibration, organic target fraction should increase with organic share of total two-phase volume, approximately as a distribution-ratio relation. The observed phase ratio near 0.19–0.22 under the nominal recipe shows that solvent addition is not itself equivalent to organic extractant volume; actual measured phase ratio will be used.

## H3 [tentative; mixing test pending]
More vigorous or longer mixing should matter mainly below equilibration and then plateau. A 1 s/100 rpm condition and a 1800 s/1200 rpm condition will bracket the nominal 300 s/600 rpm process.

## Retention hypothesis [provisionally supported for organic retention]
Across events runner-operation-0007/0010 through runner-operation-0067/0070, organic-retained final assays were broadly consistent with the preceding HPLC organic inventory, whereas aqueous inventory fell near zero after removal. Apparent closure deviations are compatible with destructive sampling and stated instrument noise; they are not treated as creation/loss. A matched nominal S2–X3 batch retaining aqueous is planned to test the converse.

## Decision
Use S2–X3 as a sensitive reference pairing for process perturbations, not as a recommendation. Remaining batches will include one nominal repeat with aqueous retention, low/high extractant phase amounts, and low/high mixing. Conclusions will be limited to tested volumes and mixing ranges.

notes.text:
# Partition study notebook

## H1 [supported within the tested material panel]
At the nominal recipe (0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous addition, 0.02 L extractant; 300 s at 600 rpm; 300 s settling), material pairing affects target partition. Pre-separation HPLC organic inventory ranged from 0.493 to 0.615 across the seven screened pairs (events runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037, -0047, -0057, -0067), while measured phase ratios were broadly similar (about 0.19–0.22). S2–X3 and S3–X2 produced 0.615 and 0.608 organic inventory, whereas S2–X2 produced 0.493. These gaps exceed the stated 0.015 standard uncertainty of one HPLC organic reading. The unexpectedly modest S2–X2 result despite favorable marginal dossier values supports pair-specific interaction rather than an index rule or purely additive marginal ranking. Only 7 of 16 combinations were tested and most once; unscreened pairs and close rankings remain unresolved.

## H2 [supported qualitatively; simple constant-D form limited]
For S2–X3 under nominal mixing, changing extractant/aqueous additions shifted measured phase ratio and organic inventory in the predicted direction. Low organic amount gave phase ratio 0.094 and organic inventory 0.434 (runner-operation-0087); the nominal repeats gave ratios 0.194/0.178 and organic inventories 0.615/0.600 (runner-operation-0037/-0077); high organic amount gave ratio 0.409 and organic inventory 0.797 (runner-operation-0097). Thus actual phase ratio, not aqueous-addition volume alone, is predictive.

A two-phase distribution-ratio diagnostic, (organic/aqueous inventory)×(1-r)/r, was about 7.68, 6.80/7.38, and 5.37 for low, nominal, and high organic amount. The nonconstant values caution against claiming a single equilibrium coefficient over this range; capacity/nonideality, recipe-dependent chemistry, and measurement closure are unresolved alternatives. The direction of the volume effect is robust, but its exact functional form is not established.

## H3 [supported as a joint mixing-intensity/time effect; components confounded]
At similar phase ratios for S2–X3, minimal mixing (1 s, 100 rpm) yielded organic inventory 0.504 (runner-operation-0107), nominal mixing yielded 0.615 and 0.600 (runner-operation-0037/-0077), and intense/long mixing (1800 s, 1200 rpm) yielded 0.714 (runner-operation-0117). The changes are large relative to 0.015 reading uncertainty and indicate that the nominal condition had not reached a demonstrated plateau. Duration and speed were changed together, so their separate roles and the true equilibrium limit are unavailable. Corresponding diagnostic distribution ratios (about 3.81, 6.80/7.38, and 9.44) should therefore be treated as apparent, mixing-dependent values rather than equilibrium constants.

## H4 [supported for phase-retention logic]
Organic-retained batches showed final-assay organic inventory broadly tracking the preceding two-phase HPLC organic inventory, with final aqueous inventory near zero (for example runner-operation-0097/-0100 and -0117/-0120). Conversely, the nominal repeat retaining aqueous changed the HPLC inventories 0.600 organic/0.376 aqueous (runner-operation-0077) to final-assay 0 organic/0.426 aqueous with phase ratio 0 (runner-operation-0080). This supports interpreting separation as physical removal of the nonrequested phase, not a sampling switch. Numerical nonclosure is expected from destructive sampling, different instrument noise, and process effects; missing or near-zero readings were not imputed.

## Predictive scope for later sealed questions
Within the tested S2–X3 ranges, increasing measured organic phase ratio should increase organic retained inventory, and stronger/longer mixing should increase transfer until an as-yet-unobserved plateau. Phase-retention choice should follow the desired inventory: retain organic when the target is predominantly organic, retain aqueous when seeking the complementary aqueous inventory. Material predictions outside the seven screened pairs are low confidence because categorical IDs are unordered and the interaction table is only sparsely sampled.

## Limits
All conclusions concern this fixed simulated initial target inventory and anonymous categories. Phase volume estimates carry 0.018 HPLC uncertainty; organic/aqueous inventories carry 0.015 HPLC and 0.01 final-assay uncertainty per reading. Replication is limited to two nominal S2–X3 HPLC runs, which agreed within 0.015 in organic inventory but had opposite final retention. No experiment independently varied mixing duration from speed, and no equilibrium time series was collected.

payload.report:
Observations: The supplied dossier described only marginal tendencies for anonymous solvents and extractants. It suggested S2 as the strongest solvent marginally and X2/X3 as promising extractants, but explicitly withheld pair interactions, phase-volume response, and mixing response. The experiments were therefore decisive.

At the common nominal recipe (0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous addition, 0.02 L extractant, 300 s at 600 rpm, then 300 s settling), the HPLC organic-target estimate depended on pairing. For S2 with X0, X1, X2, and X3 (batches 1–4), organic estimates were 0.503, 0.568, 0.493, and 0.615, respectively. With X2 and S0, S1, and S3 (batches 5–7), they were 0.506, 0.553, and 0.608. Measured phase ratios stayed in a fairly narrow 0.169–0.219 range. Thus S2–X3 and S3–X2 were the strongest tested nominal pairs, while S2–X2 was substantially weaker despite favorable marginal information. The HPLC uncertainty was 0.015 for each phase inventory and 0.018 for phase ratio, so the roughly 0.10–0.12 differences between strong and weak pairs are larger than single-reading noise. Most pairs were not replicated, however.

Batch 8 repeated nominal S2–X3 and measured 0.600 organic and 0.376 aqueous at phase ratio 0.178, close to batch 4's 0.615 organic, 0.375 aqueous, and 0.194 ratio. This repeat supports the reproducibility of S2–X3 at the resolution available.

Phase amount had a large directional effect for S2–X3 under nominal mixing. The low-organic condition in batch 9 had phase ratio 0.094 and measured 0.434 organic/0.548 aqueous. The nominal replicates gave about 0.600–0.615 organic at ratios 0.178–0.194. The high-organic condition in batch 10 had ratio 0.409 and 0.797 organic/0.214 aqueous. Thus increasing organic phase share increased the target inventory found in that phase. A simple constant-distribution-ratio diagnostic was not constant: it was approximately 7.68 at low organic amount, 6.80 and 7.38 in the nominal replicates, and 5.37 at high organic amount. The volume trend is therefore supported, but a single ideal partition coefficient is not adequate across the whole tested range. Batch 10 also showed lower HPLC purity (0.865) and higher impurity signal (0.091) than the nominal S2–X3 runs, suggesting that phase amount may alter co-extraction or composition as well as target partition.

Mixing also mattered. At similar measured phase ratios, batch 11's minimal mixing (1 s, 100 rpm) produced 0.504 organic/0.489 aqueous; nominal mixing produced 0.600–0.615 organic; and batch 12's intense, long mixing (1800 s, 1200 rpm) produced 0.714 organic/0.312 aqueous. These differences exceed measurement uncertainty. Apparent distribution diagnostics rose from about 3.81 through 6.80–7.38 to 9.44, so they behave as mixing-dependent values rather than demonstrated equilibrium constants. Because speed and duration were varied together, their individual contributions cannot be separated, and even the intense condition did not establish an equilibrium plateau.

Phase-retention behavior was consistent with physical removal of the unretained phase. For example, organic retention changed batch 10 from a pre-separation HPLC organic estimate of 0.797 to a final-assay organic estimate of 0.778 with aqueous near zero; batch 12 changed from 0.714 to 0.692 with aqueous 0.005. In the converse test, batch 8 began at 0.600 organic/0.376 aqueous, retained aqueous, and ended at final-assay estimates of 0 organic and 0.426 aqueous with phase ratio zero. Similar agreement occurred in other organic-retained batches, such as batch 7 (0.608 before separation and 0.606 final organic). Exact closure is not expected because HPLC and final assay are destructive, independently noisy measurements.

Inference: Partition is best represented as a pairing-specific, composition-dependent transfer process with a kinetic component. Material labels are categorical; their marginal dossier rankings do not combine additively. Within the tested S2–X3 domain, more organic phase shifts more target into the organic inventory, while stronger/longer mixing promotes further transfer. The phase to retain should follow the measured target location: organic retention preserves the organic inventory and aqueous retention preserves the complementary aqueous inventory.

Conjecture and alternatives: The nonconstant apparent distribution ratio could reflect finite capacity, nonideal phase composition, phase-ratio-dependent activity, co-extraction, or extraction-coupled chemistry. The mixing trend may be ordinary mass-transfer kinetics, but time-dependent reaction or degradation is a competing explanation because time and speed were confounded and composition channels also changed. Independent channel noise and imperfect mass-balance closure could explain smaller deviations but are unlikely to explain the largest controlled contrasts. The dossier could also be imperfect or misindexed, although the stronger conclusion is simply that marginal properties omit important pair interactions.

Scope and uncertainty: Only 7 of 16 material pairs were screened, mostly once; untested pairs could outperform the observed leaders. Only S2–X3 received a nominal repeat and process perturbations. No time series, independent speed-versus-duration factorial, or repeated low/high phase-volume condition was performed. Consequently, the direction of material, phase-share, mixing, and retention effects is supported within the tested ranges, but the exact functional law, equilibrium limit, generality to other pairs, and mechanistic cause remain uncertain.

payload.rationale: I treated the noiseless phase fractions as complementary and used an equilibrium-style phase-volume response calibrated to the S2–X0 and replicated S2–X3 batches, with mixing-dependent transfer interpolated from the minimal, nominal, and intense-mixing tests. The supplied marginal material information was used only for the unmeasured S0 pairings, so those intervals are wider. Q01's small organic share favors retaining aqueous; at matched conditions X3 is predicted to transfer more target than X0, favoring Q06. Intervals represent model and extrapolation uncertainty, not random HPLC noise.

payload.report:
1. No instance prior was supplied for the twelve prediction batches; the only supplied prior information was the marginal material dossier. The least secure self-developed law is the equilibrium-style phase-volume interpolation used for prediction. The campaign itself showed that the apparent distribution ratio changed with phase amount and mixing, so a constant-coefficient law was not supported. Even less tested was extrapolating from material marginals to the unmeasured S0–X0 and S0–X3 pairs: batch 3 showed that favorable marginals need not produce a favorable pair.

2. I would run one S2–X3 batch at the nominal batch-4/8 amounts, using 1800 s at 100 rpm followed by 300 s settling. I would measure pre-separation organic and aqueous target fractions, phase ratio, impurity signal, purity, and recovery by HPLC, then retain organic and obtain the final assay. This condition separates long duration from the high speed used in batch 12. An organic fraction near batch 12's 0.714, despite low speed, would shift judgment toward elapsed-time-dependent equilibration or chemistry rather than agitation-controlled transfer. A result near batch 11's 0.504 would support agitation-limited mass transfer. An intermediate result would indicate contributions from both. A target shift accompanied by substantial impurity, purity, or recovery changes would strengthen the alternative of time-dependent chemistry or co-extraction; a clean redistribution with approximate target closure would favor physical partition equilibration.

3. The impurity, purity, and recovery channels were underused in the predictive model. They could help distinguish redistribution from extraction-coupled chemistry, especially because batch 10's high-organic condition had higher impurity and lower purity. The final-assay comparisons were also used mainly to validate retention rather than to quantify cross-instrument closure. The least reliable predictions are Q01–Q06 and Q09–Q10 because S0–X0 and S0–X3 were never tested directly; Q01 and Q03 additionally extrapolate to small organic fractions. Q11 and Q12 are also weak because the campaign changed mixing duration and speed together, whereas those queries ask for a speed contrast. All queries use smaller solvent amounts than the campaign, and their omission of the campaign's reagent addition is another untested scope change, even if target fractions are normalized to fixed initial inventory.

There is a real tension between the sealed report and predictions. The report warned that a single distribution coefficient was inadequate and that marginal material rankings could fail because of pair interactions, yet the predictions used an equilibrium-style response and marginal information to estimate untested S0 pairs. The prediction rationale also interpolated mixing effects more specifically than the confounded experiments justified. Consequently, the point estimates—especially the Q06-over-Q05 decision—were pragmatic extrapolations rather than direct consequences of a validated law. This does not alter the sealed outputs; it identifies their contemporaneous evidential weakness.
